title: Severe Flooding Hits the Four Corners Region
summary:
Heavy rain that started on Wednesday has brought severe flooding to the Four Corners region, where New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Arizona meet. By Friday, October 23, floodwaters had closed roads, forced evacuations, and led to emergency declarations across all four states, and forecasters said more rain could follow through Sunday.

In San Juan County, New Mexico, emergency management spokesperson Devin Neeley described a strange contrast: light clouds and blue sky overhead, while brown floodwaters filled low-lying homes below. He said the county had not seen flooding like this in generations, and residents in vulnerable areas had been told to evacuate on Thursday afternoon.

In the southern Utah city of Hurricane, flooding damaged more than 100 homes and recreational vehicles, and the city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday. Utah Governor Spencer Cox said his heart was with affected families and urged people to follow evacuation orders.

Elsewhere, Navajo Nation police said authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency after heavy rain damaged roads, bridges, homes, and other infrastructure. In Colorado, Governor Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties and authorized National Guard members to help with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.

In Farmington, New Mexico, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said no deaths had been reported so far, and urged people not to take the flooding lightly.

Meteorologists said the rain came from the remnants of Hurricane Trudy, active in the Pacific Ocean from October 15 to 18, which formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system. Parts of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah received two to four inches of rain, while higher areas such as the San Juan Mountains received up to six inches, amounts a National Weather Service meteorologist called records in themselves.
why_it_matters: Flooding can close roads, damage homes, and force whole communities to leave, so warnings and evacuation orders protect lives and shape how regions recover.
